content:
Polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR) is an inflammatory condition that causes pain and stiffness in the shoulders, neck and hips, usually in people over 50. Stiffness is worst in the morning and can make it hard to get out of bed or lift your arms. It is treated with steroid tablets, which usually work quickly. Treatment often lasts one to two years before it can be stopped.

Symptoms

  • pain and stiffness in both shoulders, the neck, upper arms, hips and thighs
  • stiffness in the morning lasting more than 45 minutes
  • difficulty getting out of bed, dressing or lifting your arms above your head
  • tiredness, low mood, loss of appetite, weight loss or a mild fever

Symptoms usually come on over days to a couple of weeks.

Link with giant cell arteritis

Some people with PMR develop giant cell arteritis (GCA), where blood vessels in the head become inflamed. GCA can cause sight loss if not treated quickly. Warning signs include a new headache, scalp tenderness, pain in the jaw when chewing, and changes in vision. If you notice these, seek help the same day.

Who gets it

PMR almost always affects people over 50, most often over 70, and is more common in women. The cause is not known.

Diagnosis

There is no single test. Your GP will ask about your symptoms and examine you. Blood tests usually show raised inflammation (CRP or ESR). Other tests check for conditions that can look similar, such as an underactive thyroid, rheumatoid arthritis, muscle problems and some cancers. A quick response to steroids supports the diagnosis. If the picture is not clear, your GP may refer you to a rheumatologist.

Treatment with steroids

Steroid tablets, usually prednisolone, are the main treatment. Most people feel much better within days. If symptoms do not improve within about a week, the diagnosis should be reviewed.

The dose is reduced slowly over many months. This helps prevent symptoms returning and lets your body restart its own steroid production. Most people take steroids for one to two years, and some need them for longer.

  • never stop suddenly. Reduce only as advised.
  • carry a steroid card if you are given one.
  • symptoms may return as the dose is lowered. Tell your GP, as the dose may need a small increase.

Protecting your health on steroids

Long-term steroids can affect bones, blood sugar, blood pressure, weight, mood and skin. Your GP may:

  • assess your fracture risk and offer bone protection
  • check blood pressure and blood sugar regularly
  • check your eyes, as steroids can cause cataracts and glaucoma

If steroids cannot be reduced or are causing problems, a rheumatologist may suggest other medicines alongside, such as methotrexate, or a newer treatment.

Self-help

  • keep moving gently each day, as activity helps stiffness
  • strength exercises help counter muscle weakness from steroids
  • eat a balanced diet to help manage appetite and weight gain from steroids
  • get flu and COVID-19 vaccinations, as infections can be more serious on steroids
  • a hot shower in the morning can ease stiffness

Outlook

Most people with PMR recover fully, though it may take a couple of years. Relapses can happen, so keep in touch with your GP and report symptoms early.

It is normal to feel worried about taking steroids for a long time. Talk to your GP about any concerns, as they can explain how the benefits and risks balance for you and how side effects will be monitored.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:

  • a new headache with tenderness of the scalp or temples, pain in the jaw when chewing, or any change in your vision such as blurring, double vision or loss of sight — this may be giant cell arteritis and needs same-day treatment to protect your sight
  • a joint that suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel feverish or unwell (this can be a joint infection)
  • chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or signs of a stroke such as face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech

Contact NHS 111 or your GP the same day if symptoms are getting worse quickly, you cannot put weight on a leg, or you are worried and not sure where to go. If you are under a rheumatology team, use their advice line for flares and medicine questions.
